# Every point of a triangle has exact double ordinary paired depth

Let \(T\subset\mathbb R^2\) be a full-dimensional triangle of area \(V\). For \(y\in T\), let \(f_T(y)\) be its ordinary absolute halfspace depth, and let
\[
p_{TT}(y)=\inf_{\substack{u\ne0\\t\in\mathbb R}}
\left(
|T\cap\{u\cdot x\ge u\cdot y+t\}|
+|T\cap\{u\cdot x\ge u\cdot y-t\}|
\right).
\tag{1}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{\quad p_{TT}(y)=2f_T(y)\qquad(y\in T).\quad}
\tag{2}
\]
More explicitly, if \(A\ge B\ge C\) are the barycentric coordinates of \(y\), then
\[
f_T(y)=4BC\,V,\qquad p_{TT}(y)=8BC\,V.
\tag{3}
\]

This covers every triangle point, including points outside the lower diagonal vertex-to-centroid segments supplied by the earlier centered inner-simplex argument. It is not a general convex-body identity: **candidate cf676492f27e8f72** gives an exact three-dimensional square-pyramid counterexample. Nor does it identify the corresponding paired profile for higher-dimensional simplices.

All quantities here are absolute. One common continuous affine map and its constant area factor reduce the proof to normalized area \(V=1\); no integer base or lattice is modified.

## 1. Exact ordinary depth throughout a triangle

First suppose \(y\) is interior, so \(A,B,C>0\).

A cap through \(y\) containing just vertex \(i\) has edge-intercept parameters \(t_j,t_k\in(0,1]\) along the edges from \(i\) to the other vertices. Its area fraction is \(t_jt_k\), and the through-point relation is
\[
\frac{\lambda_j}{t_j}+\frac{\lambda_k}{t_k}=1.
\]
Arithmetic-geometric mean gives
\[
t_jt_k\ge4\lambda_j\lambda_k\ge4BC.
\tag{4}
\]
The same argument includes a second vertex lying on the cap boundary by allowing its intercept parameter to be one.

If the cap contains two vertices \(i,j\) and excludes vertex \(k\), its complement is a corner triangle based at \(k\). With its two intercept parameters \(t_i,t_j\), the same relation holds. Put \(v=\lambda_i/t_i\). Then
\[
\lambda_i\le v\le1-\lambda_j,\qquad
t_it_j=\frac{\lambda_i\lambda_j}{v(1-v)}.
\]
The concave quadratic \(v(1-v)\) has its minimum over this interval at an endpoint. Therefore the captured area is at least
\[
\min\left\{\frac{\lambda_k}{1-\lambda_i},
                 \frac{\lambda_k}{1-\lambda_j}\right\}
\ge\frac{C}{A+C}
=\frac{C}{1-B}
\ge4BC.
\tag{5}
\]
For the middle inequality, each ratio is of the form \(x/(x+z)\), with \(x\ge C\) and \(z\le A\). The final inequality is \(4B(1-B)\le1\). A boundary vertex does not affect area and can be included in either appropriate case.

Conversely choose the corner cap based at a vertex with barycentric coordinate \(A\), with intercepts \(2B,2C\). They lie on the edges because \(B\le1/2\). Its boundary contains \(y\), and its area fraction is exactly \(4BC\). This proves the ordinary-depth equality in (3), including all orientations. A containing cap may first be translated to pass through \(y\).

If \(y\in\partial T\), then \(C=0\), and a supporting cap gives \(f_T(y)=0\). Shift zero in (1) gives \(p_{TT}(y)=0\) as well. Hence it remains to prove (2) at interior points.

## 2. Every direction and shift has one of three possible minimum values

For a fixed nonzero normal, subtract the minimum of its three vertex heights and positively rescale their range to one. Relabel the vertices in their height order. The heights and the candidate projection become
\[
(0,a,1),\qquad
m=a\lambda_1+\lambda_2,\qquad 0\le a\le1,
\tag{6}
\]
where \((\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\) are the barycentric coordinates in this order, not necessarily their size order.

For \(0<a<1\), the normalized upper-tail function is
\[
F_a(x)=
\begin{cases}
1,&x\le0,\\
1-x^2/a,&0\le x\le a,\\
(1-x)^2/(1-a),&a\le x\le1,\\
0,&x\ge1.
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
This follows directly from the two corner-triangle area ratios. It is continuously differentiable on the whole real line.

The paired cost in this direction is \(F_a(m-t)+F_a(m+t)\). It is even in \(t\), so take \(t\ge0\). At \(t\ge\max(m,1-m)\) it equals one; thus its minimum is attained on a compact interval.

Every such minimum has one of these values:

1. \(2F_a(m)\), at shift zero;
2. \(1\), on a full/empty plateau or a constant middle regime;
3. the straddling stationary value
   \[
   J(a,m)=1-\frac{(2m-1)^2}{2a-1},
   \qquad a>\frac12,\quad \frac12\le m\le a.
   \tag{8}
   \]

Here is the complete regime check. When both thresholds lie below \(a\), the paired cost is a strictly concave quadratic in \(t\), so it has no interior minimum. When both lie above \(a\), it is a convex quadratic whose derivative vanishes only at \(t=0\). A full cap makes the cost at least one. If one cap is empty and the other proper, the cost is increasing with \(t\), so there is no new interior minimum. The tail and its derivative agree at every transition in (7), so transition minima are also stationary unless they occur at \(t=0\) or on a plateau.

In the remaining proper straddling regime,
\[
m-t\le a\le m+t,
\]
the cost is
\[
1-\frac{(m-t)^2}{a}
+\frac{(1-m-t)^2}{1-a}.
\tag{9}
\]
For \(a<1/2\) it is concave. For \(a=1/2\) it is affine; its only constant case has \(m=1/2\) and value one. For \(a>1/2\), its stationary shift is
\[
t_*=\frac{a-m}{2a-1}.
\tag{10}
\]
The support inequalities \(m-t_*\ge0\), \(m+t_*\le1\), and \(t_*\ge0\) are precisely \(1/2\le m\le a\); they also imply the stated straddling inequalities. Substitution gives (8). Thus no vertex-cut, empty-cap, or repeated-regime case has been omitted.

The first two minimum values are already at least \(2f_T(y)/V\): the first uses an actual ordinary cap, and the second uses \(f_T(y)\le V/2\). Only (8) needs a further comparison.

## 3. The straddling branch reduces to its endpoint directions

Set
\[
v=2a-1,\qquad b=\lambda_1,\qquad c=\lambda_2-\lambda_0.
\]
For the moment \(c\) is merely this scalar difference. Then
\[
2m-1=bv+c,\qquad
1-J(a,m)=\frac{(bv+c)^2}{v}
=b^2v+2bc+\frac{c^2}{v}.
\tag{11}
\]
For \(v>0\), the last expression is convex in \(v\). The feasibility conditions in (8) are exactly
\[
0\le bv+c\le v,\qquad 0<v\le1.
\tag{12}
\]
Since \(0<b<1\), this is either empty or an interval from
\[
v_0=\max\left\{0,-\frac cb,\frac c{1-b}\right\}
\]
to \(1\). When \(c=0\), expression (11) has the continuous value zero at \(v=0\). Consequently \(J\) is concave on its feasible interval and its minimum is attained at an endpoint.

At the left endpoint:

* if \(c<0\), then \(m=1/2\) and \(J=1\);
* if \(c=0\), the limiting value is again \(1\);
* if \(c>0\), then \(m=a\), \(t_*=0\), and
  \(J=1-v_0=2F_a(m)\).

All these values are at least \(2f_T(y)/V\). At the right endpoint \(v=1\), or \(a=1\),
\[
J=1-(1-2\lambda_0)^2
=4\lambda_0(1-\lambda_0)
\ge8BC.
\tag{13}
\]
To verify the last inequality without a restriction on which barycentric coordinate is \(\lambda_0\), note that every \(\lambda_i\in[C,1-C]\). Hence
\[
\lambda_i(1-\lambda_i)\ge C(1-C)=C(A+B)\ge2BC.
\]
Both endpoint values of the concave branch are therefore at least \(8BC=2f_T(y)/V\). Equations (11)–(13) prove the same bound throughout the feasible straddling branch.

This proves the paired lower bound for \(0<a<1\). For \(a=0\) or \(a=1\), approximate the repeated vertex height by heights with \(0<a<1\), keeping the barycentric coordinates and the shift fixed. The cap indicators converge outside a line, which has zero triangle area; every limiting normal remains nonzero because the height range is one. Dominated convergence extends the inequality, including supporting cuts. Taking shift zero at an ordinary minimizing cap gives the reverse bound. The proof of (2) is complete.

## 4. A nonzero-shift equality beyond the inner-simplex region

Take the standard triangle, with candidate \(y=(2/5,2/5)\). Its barycentric coordinates are \((1/5,2/5,2/5)\), so
\[
f_T(y)=\frac8{25}V,\qquad p_{TT}(y)=\frac{16}{25}V.
\]
Two barycentric coordinates exceed \(1/3\), so this point lies on none of those vertex-to-centroid segments; a vertex-anchored homothetic copy centered at \(y\) cannot be contained in the original triangle.

For the normal with vertex heights \((0,1,1)\), the candidate height is \(m=4/5\). At shift \(t=1/5\), one cap is the supporting top edge and the other has threshold \(3/5\). Their total area is
\[
0+\left[1-(3/5)^2\right]V=\frac{16}{25}V.
\]
By contrast, shift zero in this same direction costs \(18V/25\). Thus the theorem does not assert a fixed-normal Jensen inequality; the sharp comparison uses the ordinary minimum over all normal directions.

## 5. Scope and verification

Together with the elementary interval case, this proves the all-point identical-simplex identity in continuous dimensions one and two. In higher dimensions, the already proved lower-diagonal inner-simplex identity remains valid, but the present quadratic argument supplies no all-point extension. Centrally symmetric bodies have a separate all-point mechanism; the square-pyramid counterexample is neither a triangle nor centrally symmetric.

For actual mixed sources, a selected identical pair can now be paid by twice the ordinary depth at any common triangle point. Summing such independently minimized pair payments still does not retain the single base tilt linking different pairs. No global mass allocation or OC theorem is inferred.

The standard-library verifier **../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_triangle_all_point_paired_identity.py** checks the complete piecewise-quadratic minimization at rational barycentric points and normals, the exact straddling identity, endpoint inequalities, and the nonzero-shift equality. The all-real proof is Sections 1–3.
